utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there were some preliminary matters to be raised by both parties. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. First, Your Honours with respect to scheduling, earlier this week the Mladic Defence informed the Prosecution that it may use less time than originally estimated with the next witness, Mr. Edward Vullimay. With that in mind, the Prosecution has accelerated its preparations for calling the witness after that and so this is to inform the Chamber and the Defence that the Prosecution will be prepared to call Ibro Osmanovic, the next witness, as early as tomorrow morning. Then, Your Honour, yesterday I understood the Mladic Defence to be challenging the authenticity of the following exhibits. P numbers 186, 188, 189, 190, and 192. Although I do not have personal knowledge of their provenance, I have examined the records of the Office of the Prosecutor and am prepared to make the following representation about their provenance. Three of the exhibits, P186, 190, and 192, were provided to the OTP by the Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior on the 13th of December, 2004. They were provided to the investigator -- Investigator Finn Tollefsen at the Banja Luka field office on that date. The government of the RS represented to the OTP that these three documents as well as a large number of other documents handed over that day were found in the archives of the Drina Corps by the Ministry of the Interior. With respect to the two remaining documents, P188 and P189, they were obtained from the archives of the East Bosnia Corps located in Bijeljina. They were obtained from that archive during an investigative mission by staff of the OTP which took place between the 17th and 18th of May, 2004. P189 is particularly significant in that, on its face, it purports to be an order of Mr. Mladic and relates to events including the establishment of the detention camps in Eastern Bosnia during the period Susica was established. Earlier today I provided the Mladic Defence with a hard copy of P189 as well as 65 ter 06931. It is a confidential VRS order number 18/28-6, dated the 12th of June, 1992. Mr. Mladic refers to this document in his order, which is P189. I have asked the Mladic Defence to give further consideration as to whether they do in fact challenge the authenticity of P189. I note that 65 ter 6931 contains several handwritten endorsements by people that worked closely with Mr. Mladic. It may assist them in deciding whether to maintain their challenge. Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution also tenders 6931 from the bar. I do so for two reasons: As the document is incorporated into P189, the Chamber having sight of that document will be assisted in not only better understanding P189 but in assessing its authenticity. And with respect to that document it was recovered from the archives of the 1st Krajina Corps during an investigative mission in February of 1998. The Prosecution submits that the fact that a document referenced in P189 was recovered from a completely different archive is also a matter that is relevant to its authenticity. Those are my submissions, Your Honour. Thank you for giving me the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. I understood the position of the Defence yesterday to be that they said, well, prove the authenticity, but that there was no specific challenge yet to the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would -- we would kindly ask now to be taken some -- given some time to respond to these, only I want to emphasise that on the contrary what my friend across said on page 2, line 14, that -- that that's the order Mr. Mladic and relates to events including the establishment of detention camp Eastern Bosnia during the period Susica was established. On the contrary, the witness confirmed yesterday that this order has nothing to do with the establishment. It was issued after the establishment of Susica camp. So this claim is completely wrong and does not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- was not supported by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is challenged by the Defence. Could I first ask one question to Mr. Groome in relation to the authenticity. P189 -- let me see. One second, please. P189, Mr. Groome, you say how you obtained it. That means that the original is available? You know, as far as signatures are concerned, sometimes originals are of better value than copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note that it does not appear to have the signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- of just his name, and I would have to investigate whether the archive -- we did not take the original. We took, I believe, a copy, or were given a copy by the government, but I could investigate whether the original has been maintained by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. I was mainly thinking -- I now do remember it was kind of a telefax script type of document. I'm not saying that you should at this moment make further endeavours. I think it's now fully -- you have explained where you obtained them. It's now for the Defence to come up with a detailed challenge of the authenticity, if they wish to -- if they wish to persist in that matter. Mr. Lukic, we want to keep our MFI lists as short as possible. When do you think you could tell us whether there's any specific challenge to the authenticity --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have five or six filings due on Friday, so if it's possible to do it after the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in order not to spoil the whole of your weekend, Mr. Lukic, should we make it Tuesday, morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tuesday midday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that deadline is set and the Chamber will then decide after that as quickly as possible. There was another matter I do understand the Defence wishes to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Before we begin with the next witness, I do have a procedural matter that relates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will take the next witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I do understand. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Vullimay. We do have a procedural matter that relates to this witness. We did not receive the list of documents to be used in direct examination for this witness until less than 48 hours before his scheduled testimony. On 4 September 2012, at transcript page T2160, Your Honour stated that the guidance of the Chamber as it pertained to disclosure of lists of exhibits for witnesses, and as I understood Your Honours, the expectation was that the list of documents to be used in direct examination of witnesses were to be provided at least seven days before the witness is to testify. And this was after the Defence had addressed the Chamber with the problem for documents for another witness of mine that were not sent until a day or so before the testimony. Now while I've exerted more time to prepare for this witness - and I am prepared for this witness - I do need additional guidance or perhaps an order from the Chamber to ensure that with respect to other witnesses these ground rules that have been set by this Chamber are obeyed and that the parties know what recourse they have if they are not obeyed to the detriment of one party. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecution. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, Mr. Vulliamy was originally scheduled to one of the first segment witnesses in this case, and as such when we filed our list of witnesses that were being to be part of that first segment, I believe that was in April or May, we included a very extensive list of possible exhibits that would be used with that witness. So that list did go over to the Defence months ago. We have paired that potential pool of exhibits down. We've narrowed that dramatically and that's the list that we gave 48 hours ago or about 48 hours ago. I think that was on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a reduced list of a more extensive list which you provided earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would explain it, Your Honours. Wrong button. Your Honours, the list that was provided, I believe, on May the 4th was an extensive list that did not have anything more than the numbers of exhibits listed. Many of these were exhibits that had nothing to do with this witness that I did have to review and I did go through and I did eliminate. We have approximately six or seven that have now bene removed from the list and there are exhibits that are now on the list that were not on this original list that was sent in May of 2012, so I am well aware of that list and had spent a great time going through it since we could not distinguish the documents by merely their numbers being listed on the list, and I had to go through each one of them and determine that a greater part of them had nothing to do with this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, let's -- let's cut matters short. Wouldn't you think that it would have been appropriate if you reduce a list considerably - and the Chamber is not at this moment in a position to see whether there are any irrelevant documents on that list, at least I do understand that the numbers which identify the documents were there. But wouldn't you think that it would have been appropriate to provide seven days before the start of the testimony the new list?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, certainly that is the best practices and that's what we're shooting for. In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said wouldn't it have been appropriate, and then you said that would be the best practice. That -- it seems that you are not taking my comment as seriously as I intended to send it to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for that. I certainly take it very seriously. This witness has testified many times before ICTY, and there are considerable number of exhibits that are attached to him, both as associated exhibits and a great deal of videos. We have paired that number down dramatically. And I agree with you, and we should have, and it would have been been appropriate to have produced that narrowed list seven days in advance, but we have narrowed the list very, very dramatically from the original list and from what has ever been used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, I'm going to interrupt you. Of course it's appreciated that you narrowed down the list. But at the same time, if the Defence still has to work on an extensive list, then you are wasting the Defence's time and you should avoid that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, the seven days, I think, was clear, and I think where we made an exception, a possible exception, was when, during proofing, new matters would come up. Now you're describing a situation which is different from the ones in which the Chamber accepted that the list would be amended. The Prosecution should keep this clearly in mind: The seven days was our instruction. Any other matter? If not, then could the next witness be escorted into the courtroom. I take it that the OTP called it was Mr. Edward Vullimay as its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy. Would you please put on your earphones --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and could you stand for another second. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vulliamy. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you will first be examined by Ms. Bibles. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution. You find her to your right. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can I ask you to please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It is Edward Sebastian Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is it true that you've previously provided written statements to the Office of the Prosecutor and that you previously testified before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Among the previous times in which you've appeared, did you testify in the Stakic case between the 16th and 18th of September of 2002?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review the transcript of your testimony in Stakic prior to today?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I have recently.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the transport accurately reflects your testimony at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If you were asked today about the matters that were asked during your testimony in Stakic, would your answers be the same today as they were then?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, they would. And anything with which I can help the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and accurateness of your testimony in Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 28381 is Mr. Vulliamy's testimony in the Stakic case. However, it has been redacted as described in the 92 ter motion that was filed. In that transcript, we have also used grey to indicate the areas of the portion of the transcript that the Defence asked be included in their reply to our original motion. At this time I tender 65 ter exhibit 28381.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've no objection to the document being marked for identification. However, I would need the guidance of the Chamber as to -- in the past, at least with documents that the Defence has used, the Chamber has required that they be translated into Serbian -- or B/C/S I should say, the official language -- the official designation of that language in this Tribunal. This document does not have a translation into B/C/S and it's 2- and I believe -79 or -76 pages long, and it -- if it consists of evidence and testimony of this witness, I believe that the -- my understanding of the prior practice of this Chamber is that this would have to be translated. So again, no objection to being marked for identification, but unless the Chamber has more guidance for me I would ask for it to be translated before it's accepted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of previous testimony used as a 92 ter statement, it's my understanding that there is the B/C/S audio of the testimony and that the written transcript has not been required in the past. I do believe this is the first transcript that we have admitted in this particular trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will MFI the transcript. And, Mr. Ivetic, if you could give the Chamber examples of where transcripts were translated into B/C/S before being used, because you were talking about documents, and, of course, this is a very specific kind of a document - this is a transcript - where, I think, it's known to everyone that the B/C/S audio does exist. So if you could provide us with examples of transcripts being translated and then provided in hard copy, the Chamber would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know of none offhand. The documents I was referring were tendered exhibits that were in English as an original language. I would note, however, that the B/C/S audio, it's my understanding, is not linked to this exhibit for purposes of the record. That would perhaps be another way. I am thinking in terms of the -- my understanding of Your Honours' ruling with respect to having documents translated was that the official record needed to have both languages of the documents and therefore if -- if there's an audio -- if the audio is introduced into the record that might resolve the issue. That's why I was asking for more instructions from the Chamber on this specific issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that. But I think it would have been wiser that you would have introduced the matter as a transcript issue rather than a document issue, which would have focussed our discussion immediately on the matter you apparently want to raise. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28381 becomes Exhibit P199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Ms. Bibles, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave I will read a summary of Mr. Vulliamy's written testimony. The actual evidence is, of course, available to the public in the form of this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Edward Vullimay worked as a journalist for the London based "The Guardian" newspaper in 1992. By July of 1992, Mr. Vulliamy was aware of the presence of a camp called Omarska in northern Bosnia when he heard Radovan Karadzic publicly deny rumours about the camp and invited the media to see this camp. Mr. Vulliamy went to Belgrade in July of 1992, the end of July, and was -- with other reports was flown by the military to Pale where he spoke directly with Karadzic who promised to grant access to Omarska camp in Prijedor, as well as other camps. Mr. Vulliamy and Penny Marshall travelled by vehicle with a military escort in the Republika Srpska and a VRS officer Milutinovic. In Prijedor, they saw massive destruction of the village of Kozarac and Milutinovic explained that 40.000 Muslims had decided to leave the area. The journalists had a long meeting in Prijedor with a group comprised of local Serb leaders and military leaders who tried to dissuade them from visiting Omarska. While waiting outside this meeting, Mr. Vulliamy saw a long line of Muslim women lined up and he spoke with them and learned that they were trying to find out information about their husbands, brothers, and sons, who had either disappeared or been detained. At the end of this, the journalists were taken to Omarska and were given a very restricted tour, seeing only a group of men brought into the canteen for food. Mr. Vulliamy's testimony was that the condition of the men was shocking. When Mr. Vulliamy attempted to venture out to a hangar in the location of the detainees, he was stopped and a confrontation occurred with the end result being that he was not allowed to see the parts of Omarska that he was most interested in viewing. The journalists were then taken to Trnopolje where the witness described in detail a barbed wire fence and behind it a crowded group of men, many who were skeletal and in a serious state of decay. The witness testified to the conditions in the detention facilities and the treatment of non-Serb detainees in these facilities. After visiting the Trnopolje camp, the journalists left for Belgrade. In Belgrade, the witness described a conversation that he had with Nikola Koljevic in which Koljevic makes fun for the western media for having been so focussed on Sarajevo and not finding the camps for so long. On the 7th of August, 1992, the witness's article on the visit to the camps was published in the British newspaper, "The Guardian," and he describes in his testimony the dramatic response to the article and the impact of this discovery. The witness describes that he went into the Republika Srpska in mid-August of 1992 to try to determine where the refugees were going after Croatia closed its doors to refugees. He ended up in a deportation convoy of Muslims from Sanski Most and travelled with them through Banja Luka and over Mount Vlasic and through the front lines to Travnik. The witness describes returning to Bosnia after the Dayton Agreement was signed and he observed the conditions and the denial of the camps' existence, the very camps he had visited in 1992. Your Honours, this concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague noted that on page 13, line 24, that the transcript is not complete, but it will be reviewed on the basis of the audio, I take it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I would like to begin by having you update your professional biography in terms of what you've done since 2002.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Briefly I moved back to the United Kingdom and worked as a general reporter for the -- mostly for "The Observer" newspaper, related to "The Guardian" on a number of issues, I -- I researched in some depth and wrote a book about the terrible drug war in Mexico and spent much time down there. Perhaps more relevantly, I also kept up research on the matters that are before the Court today over a period of years and worked towards a book on the aftermath of -- of this discovery of the camps which was published which involved, as it were, going back over a lot of the ground since I made the statement -- the testimony which has been entered before you. And working based in London for the same newspaper doing the same job, basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like you to go back to July of 1992. Do you recall what it was that you heard Karadzic describe about how was being held in the camps in northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, the initial denial from Dr. Karadzic was that there were no civilians being held in these camps. And this was a point he stressed, as well as denying the conditions that were alleged to pertain in Omarska according to the reports that were at issue at the end of July when he came to London, and Trnopolje which had also been -- the name of which had been put into the public domain. As we proceeded, the -- guard me on how far you want me to go in answering the question. But initially the idea was -- the -- the conditions reported were untrue, there were no civilians, and as we got to further down the line, there were various other, as it were, various other accounts given that there were prisoners of war here, that military fighters were in this place, civilians in that. But initially the idea was that there are no civilians being detained in any camps. That was the line we were being given.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In your testimony, and it's on e-court page 11, you describe that you flew from Belgrade to Pale in early August. Could you please describe for us who transported you by air?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. After some five days of being delayed in Belgrade, we were transported by a military helicopter which I presumed, because we were in Belgrade, to be a federal military helicopter, but I don't know if it was a Bosnian Serb military helicopter. It was a military helicopter and we were being transported by men in para -- in military fatigues. And that was on the morning of the 3rd of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you flew over Eastern Bosnia, were you able to see the ground from your position in the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I've written and testified to this. We got a view out of a window of a fairly shocking landscape below of towns and villages which had been completely incinerated and appeared to be deserted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Just sort of jump ahead in time, were you ever in that same part of the country after Dayton was signed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. This was logically Eastern Bosnia, and looking back, I can figure out that it was the -- it was a terrain behind the -- the -- the towns on the Drina of Visegrad and around that area. The hinterland behind there. And Foca. And I did go back in the beginning of 1996 in the first opportunity that I could after the war was over to research what had been going on in those -- in those places that one could only see in 1992 from the air, and indeed it was as one had worse feared from looking at them - I worked mostly on Visegrad on that point - and, yes, there were stories of -- and proven stories of families being locked in houses and incinerated alive, people thrown off the bridge at -- in that town and mass executions there, and the systematic mass violation of women at camps set up for that purpose. So in the hindsight in 1996, one was able to make some sense of the -- of what we saw from the helicopter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask, Your Honours, that the other side direct me to where in the 65 ter summary Visegrad is identified among the areas that would be lead for this witness. In item 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I stop you there. The problem is not with the Prosecution. The problem is with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing you were asked: Were you in that same part of the country after Dayton was signed? So I think the answer should be yes or no. But what Ms. Bibles would like to know what you saw, noticed, who you met, what the weather was, et cetera, wait for her next question. And then it will be clear to you what specifically she would like to know about your later visit to the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, this is, if I say the problem is with the witness, but you are in a position to avoid --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that it happens. Clear, focussed questions will avoid this kind of problems. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to August 3rd of 1992 and your meeting with Radovan Karadzic in Pale. Which places did he promise you access to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We met with Dr. Karadzic and he guaranteed us access to Omarska and to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were these the locations that you asked to see?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, with special emphasis on Omarska which was the main place at issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you travelled to Prijedor -- excuse me, how you travelled from Pale to Banja Luka? Could you describe what kind of vehicles you were in.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. We were in initially a military vehicle, a khaki camouflaged truck, people-mover, with -- accompanied by - and it was a convoy - accompanied by in various vehicles, two, perhaps three: Vice-president Koljevic and a Bosnian Serb television crew wearing military fatigues, some of them, and a military Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you have been able to travel into the areas of northern Bosnia without the military escort?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I very much doubt it. Because it was a war zone, as everybody kept telling us. That was obvious. And the journey from Pale to -- as it turned out to be Banja Luka, turned out to go through a very narrow corridor across northern Bosnia which would absolutely have required a military escort and, indeed, military permission to be there at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Once you were in Banja Luka, did you become aware of a military representative being appointed to escort you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, just -- sorry to interrupt. Isn't this in detail in the transcript of the testimony in the Stakic case? So we do not need to hear again what is clearly on the transcript. So I wonder whether it was because of the colour of the cars that you did put those questions, that there was no free travelling, I think that transpires from all of that as well and I think is not in dispute at this moment, that people were not freely moving around. So, therefore, could you please focus on what we do not know yet from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, in Stakic -- the difference between his testimony in Stakic and this one is we have more emphasis on some of the military features than were highlighted or detailed in his testimony. I'll fine-tune my questions in those particular areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Keep in the back of your mind our observations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you aware of a military representative being appointed specifically to escort your visit?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Apart from the people who had been with us all along, not until he arrived, and that would have been on the morning of August the 5th when we were in Banja Luka and we were introduced to Colonel Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether you have followed his career since the time you were with him on August 5th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, because he played an important part in the day, I obviously asked, well, you know, what happened to him, and in casual conversations, and someone said that they heard he had gone to Han Pijesak to work on the General Staff under General Mladic but I had no way of confirming that. It was just as a matter of interest that I asked and I still don't know if that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I want to go now to the meeting that had you in Prijedor with the Crisis Staff. Could you describe for us the interaction between the military who were present in the meeting and the political leaders in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, Milutinovic took us to the -- to the municipal headquarters in Prijedor, and the body was assembled, Crisis Staff, crisis committee, whatever we call it, and it was made up of three -- one police chief, two -- the -- the president and the vice-president, and the military component in that committee was introduced to us as a Colonel Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you describe for us once you went to Omarska the contact between the military escorts that were with you and the Omarska staff?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, we were taken to Omarska by Colonel Milutinovic in a vehicle that he now boarded that had been rented by ITN, and then he handed us over, where Drljaca, the police chief, was in another vehicle, and then he handed us over to them and to the camp commander before the briefings began.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And can you describe what the relationship was between Milutinovic and the Omarska staff?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, at the time we weren't making any particular distinctions between them, but, I mean, it appeared to be seamless.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You've previously testified that you saw a group of detainees at Omarska. Is this depicted on film?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, ITN were filming in Omarska that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will now play a portion of the video-clip with 65 ter 2239 B using Sanction. Your Honours, this is a clip that is six minutes long, and in the interest of time my intention is to show Mr. Vulliamy just a few short extracts of the six-minute clip and then at the end tender the entire clip. It is a video that Mr. Vulliamy viewed in proofing, and while it is almost identical to footage in associated exhibit 65 ter 22393A, which is an associated exhibit, it does have a few minutes of additional footage involving Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could you just check with the transcript. Were you referring to the video you intend to play as 22393B?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Now I'm looking at my -- yes. Now those are only associated exhibits. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart, if you could play the video from the beginning and pause it at 1 minute, 11 seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have -- do you want us to listen to the audio as well? Then it should be played twice in accordance with the newest rules or at least the draft rules on the production of video material in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Your Honours, I'll add that the booths do have the transcripts B/C/S and English transcripts of these clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we first play the whole of the video and then the second time it will be played where it will be translated in B/C/S as well. And I would say in the second round, you ask the video to be stopped at a certain time and then ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I say the whole, I mean the whole selected portion in 22393B. Yes. And that's not the whole of the -- it's not the entire video. I do understand that. Please, let's first look at the footage as a whole. Mr. Mladic wants to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps while my colleague is consulting, perhaps I can ask one question: I understood counsel to say that the whole video was going to be tendered, do we then not need to confirm the translation of the whole video using the new procedure if the whole video is indeed being tendered into evidence and will be relied upon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think we focus at this moment at the portion to be played today and that we have transcript -- could Mr. Mladic please lower his voice. Mr. Mladic, please. Mr. Ivetic, I suggest that we start because it will be without translation at this moment, and in the second round I take it consultation will be concluded. Let's play the footage you have selected, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Ms. Marshall: The Bosnian Serbs don't call Omarska a concentration camp. Come in, they challenged ITN, and see it for yourselves. Under Serbian armed guard for our own protection, a three-day journey ended here, at the gates of a disused mine in northern Bosnia. Here we were shown only several hundred of the two and a half thousand prisoners or Muslim men at Omarska, we were told, to be interrogated. Those found guilty of fighting Serbs were then sent to prisoners of war camps; innocents to refugee camps. "This is all we saw of the prisoners and of Omarska itself. They never spoke; the only voices, those of the guards ordering them to eat faster and leave. "How are you treated, what are the conditions, I asked. "Prisoner: I don't want to tell lies. I can't speak the truth. Thank you for coming."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We'll proceed with the second playing of the transcript [sic] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll look at it again and it will now be translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did you speak with any detainees other than the one that was just depicted in the video at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke to him. I'm in the film. And I did speak to one other, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will now play another portion of this same video-clip from 1 minute 39 seconds, to 2 minutes, 22 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that known under the same 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Ms. Marshall: And then the men left back to wherever they'd come from, away from our cameras and questions, hidden from the United Nations and the Red Cross who have been denied access to Omarska, hidden until now from the world. We were not allowed to follow them to their living accomodation, what appeared to be the larger of the two buildings to see the other 2.000 detainees and how they lived. "What's your reason? "Serbian Woman: I'm trying to do my best here. "Ms. Marshall: ... not to show us where they live? "Mr. Williams: When Dr. Karadzic... Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promise to us? "Serbian Woman: He promised us something else and said: 'You can do this and this and that, and not that.' "Ms. Marshall: We've seen nothing. We see one dining room with 80 prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Your Honours, under the protocol we'll go back and play that segment again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it will now be translated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, we've stopped this clip at 2 minutes -- sorry. We've stopped this clip at 2 minutes 22 seconds. Do you recognise the man on the left side of the screen wearing the hat?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's Colonel Milutinovic with whom we'd been all day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What position did Milutinovic take with respect to your request to go to other areas of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We were trying to get into the hangar where we suspected the atrocities to be taking place, and he was one of the three men - two of them here - who stopped us from doing so, and they were backed up by guards who are behind them who took the safety catches off their guns as we tried to approach the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, could I invite you to wait a second before you start answering the question because the translators and the transcribers need some time to first finish the question and then -- and your speed of speech, if that could be reduced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll wait and slow down, sir. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At the time that you were at the Omarska depicted here, could you determine whether the detainees were military soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: At the time they appeared -- there was no reason to suppose that they were soldiers. No reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At the time you were at Omarska, did you see any women detainees?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Whether they were detainees or not at the time, we were unable exactly to tell because the only women we saw at the time were serving the meal, if that's what you could call it. But my research has subsequently found they were doing other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll -- go on then. Did you, in your later research and interviews, determine that there were, in fact, women detainees?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would object and ask where this evidence is identified in the Rule 65 ter summary or in the prior transcripts in five cases that this witness has testified to. It's a new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what exactly is it? Because women serving food, I think, was in the transcript of the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we're talking about research --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Research.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- and the results of his research. Research was identified but not the results thereof or the bases therefore and that has not been disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we -- Ms. Bibles, you asked the witness to provide us with what -- what he determined on the basis of his research. Let's take it step by step and let's see whether the witness has any -- gained any knowledge after that and not ask for conclusions yet. At the same time, if you could respond to Mr. Ivetic's complaint, as a matter of fact, that he is not aware of any research you would ask about. Please do that first.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We did provide that the witness would testify about statements made to him by various officials, people on all sides of the conflicts, as well as international organisations regarding the nature and purpose of the conflict. He has testified regarding the fact that he went back into Bosnia after -- actually throughout the war and then after Dayton was signed, that he has spoken with a great deal of individuals regarding the events at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, the Chamber will carefully monitor your next questioning but doesn't stop you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you subsequent to your 1992 visit to Omarska interview people and other organisations with respect to whether or not women detainees were present in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes in detail and at length, and I have concluded that they were being kept prisoner and for serial violation above the canteen where we were filming and where they were serving the soup. They were being raped.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, after Omarska, how were you transported to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We were -- we were evicted from Omarska and we were transported to Trnopolje in the company of Milutinovic, but we didn't see him after we arrived and we were in ITN's vehicle by that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And were portions of your time at Trnopolje filmed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will now play another portion of this same video, 65 ter 22393B. We would play a clip from 2 minutes, 22 seconds, to 4 minutes 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: "Ms. Marshall: And so we left. Our hosts fulfilling their promise to show us the second camp, Trnopolje, where 2.000 refugees are living. We were not prepared for what we saw and heard there. "Several hundred said that they had arrived from Omarska that morning or from another detention camp, released to this refugee centre, after days, sometimes months of interrogation. We asked if the allegations of beating in the detention centres were true. "Prisoner: We've seen much about that. We've seen people were hungry, that's true. "Prisoner: I'm not sure that I'm allowed about that, you know. I'm... Can you understand me? "Ms. Marshall: Tell us the truth. "Prisoner: I'm afraid. 250. "Ms. Marshall: Killed? What happened? "Ms. Marshall: In this vicious civilian war where atrocities against Serbs as well as Muslims occur daily, finding the truth isn't easy. We ourselves saw no evidence of beating on any refugee here. We only heard the allegations, allegations even camp doctors seemed unable to substantiate in front of our Serb hosts. "Does he have any cases of people who were being beaten from the other camps? "Interpreter: Many.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARSHALL
utterances.text: Many? Would he be happier speaking his own language? "Interpreter: Yes. "Ms. Marshall: I was able, however, to smuggle out a roll of film, and the man who took these pictures and gave it to me said he would be killed if caught. He begged me to check if in three days he was still alive."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll now we'll now replay that segment for B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm looking and I see that it may be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Bibles, apart from that, just to clarify the record, this video was played twice. It is only the first time that the English original appears on the transcript. When we play it again it is orally translated into French and into B/C/S, but the transcript does not, again, reflect the English words spoken in this video footage. Could I, apart from that, ask you, your last estimate was two hours, I think. Are you on track?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do not expect to take that full time, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, if we take a break, we will resume at five minutes to 11.00, that you'll conclude not any later than five minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We take a break for 20 minutes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of the doctor that we just saw on the video?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In Trnopolje, his name is Idriz Mrdjanic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is the clip that we just saw, was that the first time you were aware of the presence of another camp in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived at the fence, we heard about what for me was the third camp of which I was aware -- sorry, the fourth camp of which I was aware, which was called Keraterm, where the men behind the wire were talking about a massacre. I called it Kerata. At the time I wrongly noted it, but I now know it to be Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you reviewed the entire six minutes of this clip of video that we've seen portions of today?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Does it accurately depict the scenes at Omarska and Trnopolje on the 5th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The clips of Omarska show the little that we saw and the clips of Trnopolje accurately reflect what I recall from there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 22393B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understood we do have a B/C/S translation of that so then there will be no objection to that being tendered in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22393B becomes Exhibit P200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P200 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that we be shown 65 ter 06981. And I'd ask that we see page 1 of both the B/C/S original and the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you've testified that your conversation with Radovan Karadzic was the 3rd of August of 1992 regarding your visits to these camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. 3rd of August, we met Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you describe whether you were with -- how many were in your group of reporters, how many journalists?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was myself plus Penny Marshall and Ian Williams, two from ITN reporters, and two crews. It would have been a total of -- seven or eight of us in total.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And referring to the second-to-the last line of the document that you see in front of you, regarding the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe the role that Milutinovic had with you as being consistent with this order?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Lack of foundation and calls for speculation. First of all, we have not established when is the first time this gentleman saw this order, as I believe in testimony that I've read, it will make -- be the determinative factor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please find a foundation for -- and perhaps first explore the matter without referring to a certain document, pointing the witness at a part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, my intent was not, I think as counsel is alluding, to tender this document. Simply to mark it for identification at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you were asking to describe the role of Milutinovic, whether it was consistent with this order. I would have started with asking what his role was in this and this context, rather than to first give a document and then compare it with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the page reference, but I believe the witness has already testified to that this morning about the role of Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then there's no -- I need a page reference to verify that. But please proceed at this moment and try to avoid any speculation or -- also try to avoid the witness to read what his answer is supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you have a military escort during your time at the camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, we were -- we were -- we had a military escort throughout from Pale, and we were specifically assigned to Colonel Milutinovic in Banja Luka from the morning of the 5th of August, which the day -- the day we went to the camps and he accompanied us in our vehicle, explained the background about what we saw, and accompanied us to the Municipal Assembly headquarters and to the camps. And he departed at some point around the time of our arrival at Trnopolje. He was there throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: During your time in Prijedor and with the camps, did you have the co-operation of the military forces that -- that you saw?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, at this point I would simply tender or mark this order for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this witness has not testified as to anything as to documents, so I don't understand why it's being marked for identification with this witness. I don't believe it's [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you consider that it's more appropriately tendered as from the bar table because it relates to the same matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then the Defence would have an ability to respond in writing to bar table submissions, as has been the practice in prior cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification. The Chamber will consider whether and at what moment in time it would be appropriate to seek it -- to tender it from the bar table. We said at the end of the -- at a later stage. At the same time, we are looking now, repeatedly, at documents which are very directly linked to a witness, to the testimony of a witness, so we may further consider what the appropriate timing for such documents is. Madam Registrar, it would be marked under what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06981 becomes Exhibit P201, Your Honours, MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P201 keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I'd like to next go through just to ask some follow-up details regarding your mid-August 1992 experiences with the convoy to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this reference is in e-court, pages 85 to 91.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, as you approached the front line on Mount Vlasic, could you describe for us whether there was military activity actually happening at the front line?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, as we approached the front line in this convoy, after a terrifying day, we -- the police which had been escorting the convoy essentially turned back. That was when we, as it were, declared who we were, and we were offered by the police a chance to go back with them. We did not want to do that. And we were then -- accompanied this convoy of deportees towards the front lines, with, as I say, extreme trepidation, and by then we were in the hands -- I mean, this was the military front line by then, so they would have been fighters, soldiers, manning the front lines as the convoy went through their front lines, were stopped at their front lines, their cars taken away from them and other possessions, and they were sent out across the no man's land, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And specifically can you describe for us the individuals who were controlling the front line on the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: They were in uniform, camouflage fatigues. They were a fairly rough lot. They were taking, as I say, the cars of the -- of the deportees away, to turn back into the territory through which we'd come. They added to the atmosphere of total fear, I have to say. I mean, we didn't know where we were going and nor did they, except by then it was obvious we were going across a no man's land which is rule number 1: You don't cross the lines, you don't do it. So they were -- yes, they were abrasive, and then we managed to parley with them in order to keep our car by, if you will pardon me for putting it this way but that's how things are, we decided to discuss a football game that team had recently won in a cup final and that defused the situation slightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And the individuals you were dealing with, could you describe the uniforms of the individuals that you've just talked about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Military, khaki camouflage fatigues.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In your Stakic testimony, Your Honours, at e-court page roughly 91, you describe or you talk about the arrival of the convoy in Travnik. I'd like to ask just a couple of details to follow up. You have in your testimony talked about the number of people that were in the convoy, but you didn't mention in your previous testimony the number of refugees present in Travnik. Were you able to determine that when you were in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. While we'd been on the convoy, by definition we had no idea who or what or where we were going. It was on the road in the no man's land that I realised that other people had certainly come this way before because there were -- well, body parts in the road at one point. There was fighting on the road. We were crossing line, shells, landing nearby, and it was mined. But when we got into Travnik, one got a sense of the scale and regularity of this because as the deportees sought spaces to camp down on the floors of the gymnasium school and other facilities that had been arranged, they -- I mean, there was very little space. These places were already packed with others. All of them clearly civilians, families, elderly people, children, and one then obviously got a sense of the scale of what was going on but also its regularity. It turned out that we had just been yet another night, yet another convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And approximately how many refugees were in Travnik when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I was -- we were given a figure of something like 36.000 by then. This was mid-August. I returned to Travnik many times and that figure accumulated with time, right up to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then going on, you've testified and you testify in Stakic that you had returned to the area after Dayton and you've continued to interview people from Prijedor over time. Are you aware of whether there are still missing people from Prijedor, and, if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This, I believe, was not disclosed. It's not in the Rule 65 ter summary and it was not testified to in any of the prior five cases, I believe, that the witness - maybe six - that the witness participated in. And I don't believe it was disclosed to the Defence in terms of being able to know what the results of this research is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, actually, he did testify. Unfortunately, I don't have an e-court number handy. On the original transcript, it appears to be page 7990. He describes still the missing people and compares the missing people from Srebrenica and I believe Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's e-court page 93, if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was quite happy with the transcript page, as a matter of fact. Was that 7990?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you say Prijedor people still missing should be discussed there. Let me have a look. 1996, returned to Prijedor. On that page, the return to Prijedor is dealt with. And also the witness wanting to go back to Omarska, just after Dayton. But I do not find, at this moment, at least at this page, anything about persons still missing in Prijedor, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. And up above, the witness describes that he had been commissioned to research and to do a series of long articles retracing his steps of the war and to try to flesh out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where is that? Could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Lines, if you start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That same page. Lines, I believe, it's 1 through -- 1 through 10, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He sat together with the editor and what he would do next and retrace some steps of the war. That is not a clear reference to -- to -- to how many people are still missing in Prijedor after the war, is it? Let me check with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your mike, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is sustained. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am. Just one moment to re-adjust myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you will now be cross-examined by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have the assistance of the usher, I have videos that might be used in cross-examination and the practice has been to distribute to the Prosecution copies for their convenience as they have done for us at the beginning of their direct. And while we're waiting for that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, we can proceed since that does not have anything to do with our discussion as of yet. Sir, as you've heard my name is Dan Ivetic, and while I appreciate that you have testified in several proceedings here, I want to caution you: Since we both speak the same language, we have to observe a pause between question and answer and permit the court reporter and translator to do their jobs. I know in the past that has been an issue for both yourself and myself.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I've been rightly reprimanded in many -- many directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As have I. Now, likewise, I assure you that if you focus your answers to deal directly with the questions that I pose to you, we will get through this in as little time as possible. Is that fair, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, you did not ask, but I feel I should give you an estimation of the time that I am going to be using with this witness. We had previously estimated seven hours, that is no longer the case, and I anticipate being able to finish within four hours which would still leave time tomorrow for redirect and anything else with respect to this witness within the time period that he was made available to testify. I know this is in excess of the 2.5 hours that are normally foreseen for Rule 92 ter witnesses; however, I state that this a case where we have a three-day transcript of 276 pages as the Rule 92 ter statement and we have multiple associated and other exhibits with this witness, and that is why the time that we would be seeking would be in excess of the 2.5 hours and would be four hours in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If everyone tries. It's best that we conclude tomorrow. That will be fine. Apart from that, the Prosecution claimed for more time as well, Mr. Ivetic. Therefore, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, first I would like to just briefly go through your background somewhat so we can better understand where you're coming from in particular parts of your testimony. Am I correct that your educational degrees are in politics, philosophy, and economics? ?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, one of my degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. You said one of your degrees. Just for completeness, could you tell me about any other degrees that I have missed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The other is in the area of art history, Your Honours. I'm not sure if it's of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that you have no educational degrees in criminal justice or police work?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No -- sorry, you are correct: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the time that you first went to Bosnia-Herzegovina in August of 1992, at that time you were not conversant in the Serbo-Croatian language as it was then called, were you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I could not speak it. I had pigeon B/C/S, whatever it is it, by 1995. I don't speak it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that you were reliant upon a translator for the entirety of your visits to Prijedor in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: During that visit, yes. There were two translator, principally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if my recollection serves me well, I've read the answers of all the last three questions, even in detail, pigeon knowledge of -- that's what I've read already.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. There's no need to present repetitious evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the visits -- the one visit, or that visit, if I direct your attention to the visit of February 1996 to Prijedor, were you also reliant upon a translator at that point?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn a bit to focus on journalism, which is your profession. Would you agree with me the proposition that a basic tenant of journalism is to report the facts that you see accurately and truthfully as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about the proposition that as a journalist one has to objectively report the facts. Would you agree with that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Objectively, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm waiting for the transcript. And, again, sir, we have to pause between question and answer to make the jobs of the court reporter and translator easier. Do you consider yourself to be objective as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Objectivity inasmuch as it's fact-specific, yes, I do consider myself objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How about in terms of your testimony -- strike that. How in terms of your reporting relating to Bosnia-Herzegovina and here let's limit it to the Prijedor municipality in August of 1992, were you considering yourself to be objective at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think I've objectively reported what I saw and heard and have done since. I have not always been neutral over what I have seen and learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We will explore the differences between those two terms, and I hope to have your intake on some confusing words that I found being attributed through you in print to see if we can sort through this and find out what it is exactly that you mean by distinguishing between "objectivity" and "neutrality."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have Exhibit 1D262 up in e-court. And this is -- the part that I'm looking at is page 5 of the same towards the middle of the page. Sir, while we wait for that, for your information this a publication of "CounterPunch" magazine, and I'm not interested in what these authors, Mr. Herman and Mr. Peterson, say about the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I am interested in certain quotations that they attribute to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Madam Registrar informs me that the document you want on the screen is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the information we have is that it is in e-court. We've been dealing with the technical services for a number of days now with problems with e-court. I do have hard copies, enough I believe for Your Honours, and the booths, the witness, and opposing counsel. If we can proceed on that bases then we can hopefully have the document released in e-court or whatever is the holdup technically but still proceed with the testimony in an efficient manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can proceed in this way. At the same time it should be explored why you think it's in e-court and why the Registry thinks it's not in e-court. That should be established quickly, but let's proceed on the base of the hard copies to be distributed by the Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, while that's being distributed, again I, for purposes of information this is a printout from "CounterPunch" magazine and it's dated 2009. The authors of the article are Mr. Herman and Mr. Peterson, and I'm not that interested in what they have to say about the conflict, but I want to ask you about certain citations or quotations that they attribute to yourself to see if that is, indeed, your position as to objectivity and neutrality or if they have misreported it and, if so, that you can clarify for us. And for your benefit, it's on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my colleague indicates that I guess copies were not given to the booths. Three copies were given to the Prosecution. I had made copies for the booths, so I don't know if that would assist the translators since it's not up on the screens. I will be guided by Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We still have the old fashioned way of using the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Spoken word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh. The ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the ELMO. I had forgotten even the name of it. It's so rarely used. Could it be put on the ELMO. And to the extent that there are still copies available to be distributed to the booth -- no. And the Judges would be willing to make their copies available - in limited numbers - to the booth, to the extent needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe my questions will be limited to specific quotations that I will be reading into the record so that might also assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have it at page 5. Could you please slowly proceed. Apparently the ELMO is not yet functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I could have your assistance to see if this accurately reflects things you have written or said. The first quote I want to ask you about is there in middle, and it starts off: "There are times in history when neutrality is not neutral at all but complicity in the crime." Does this accurately reflect a position that you have taken either in print or verbally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do we find it exactly, Mr -- could you be a bit more precisely, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would be the middle of the third paragraph of the actual article on page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm happy to discuss the issue in -- you know, in so far as Their Honours are, you know, prepared to listen to a political discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I do think that there are times when neutrality is complicit. I think that the neutrality of the international community during the war in Bosnia was one of those. There are others. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be -- first of all, the question was whether this reflects your position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On -- on some occasions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in history, generally, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in that same paragraph, the next quote begins: "I do not want to be neutral between a camp guard and the inmate, the women raped seven times a night every night and the beast who rapes her." Does that accurately reflect a position that you have taken in writing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I to take that the first part of the quote is referring to the situation in Omarska and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Not necessarily specifically but to the situation that pertained at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say, and I take that the first part of the quote is referring to -- by the first part, do you mean the part that says: "There are times in history..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I guess to be clear, sir, is that how you understood my question and is that how your answer was phrased?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. It's about times in history, not specifically that one only. It could be Rwanda, but we're discussing Bosnia. And, yes, that is an accurate statement of how I felt and how I feel, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the second quotation, are those comments of yours directly relating to Omarska and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, and generically the camps as existed up until the point that that was written that I knew about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And although it is not written in this particular piece, I think you alluded to it in your earlier comments, but did you author a piece in April 1998 entitled: "I Must Testify. Why One Journalist is Giving Evidence Against Alleged War Criminals in Bosnia." And there you can continued on by saying: "That was the cowardly and callous neutrality adopted by the UN itself in Bosnia to such disastrous and bloody effect." Do you affirm these words, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the language is strong but I still think that the performance of the United Nations in allowing the slaughter to continue, as it did, was cowardly and in some ways callous, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to return to this document. In the same paragraph a few lines down, they -- they attribute a quote from the British Journalism Review wherein you apparently said that you were embarrassed by how objective you had been. Do you -- can you affirm that this something that you said?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. I have never read anything in the British Journalism Review. If I did say that -if, I haven't read it, and I know I used the term "objective" in that respect at the introduction to a book I wrote in 1993 - I have said this to the Court before. I'll say it again if Their Honours want to hear it. I have -- I was confusing that, "neutrality," "objective," I am -- I -- what I meant was I am embarrassed by how neutral I had been over -- in some of the reporting, with hindsight.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: At the start one continued to try one's best to see a balance in things, and these -- this balance is in my early reporting, even when we found the camps. I'm quite embarrassed by that. Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
