utterances.text: Okay. If we can continue on, there's another quotation attributed there to you that says -- beginning: "With Omarska and Trnopolje, objective coverage of the war became a rather silly notion." Does this quote accurately reflect the position that you have held and/or published?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: This is "CounterPunch," which is neither neutral nor objective, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about, sir. Is the position that you've taken --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't find the quote, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: And I don't think I would have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is in the -- it is in the middle of the third paragraph that says: "At least since 1993 when he wrote in the British Journalism Review that he was 'embarrassed about how objective he used to be' but 'with Omarska and Trnopolje, objective coverage of the war became a rather silly notion.' Vulliamy proclaimed that was he now 'on the side of the Bosnian Muslim people against a historical and military programme to obliterate hem.'"

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that a position that you have taken and/or published, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, this is "CounterPunch" quoting the British Journalism Review, which I haven't seen, quoting me. I did, during the three years of experiencing that war in Bosnia as a reporter and as a human being, come to take the side of what I saw as the resistance to what was happening against the perpetrators of the people who were doing it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- although I do not know that it's not a quote of yours, but just to understand the gist of it about silly notions: Would objective coverage become a rather silly notion or neutral coverage? Because you earlier said that you had perhaps used not the right term at this moment. So if you say you were siding, did you consider this, that it would be silly to be neutral or silly to be objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour. Because I'm -- I'm admitting that I have, as it were, crossed the terms in the past when somebody rings you up on the phone for an interview or whatever. Yes, thank you. I, inasmuch as objectivity is fact-specific, it is what you see. That is never a silly notion. To continue to have remained neutral over what I had seen and what was clearly going on over those three years -- well, "silly" is not very good word. It doesn't make sense to me as a human being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So irrespective of whether the quote is accurate or not, this is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my position, yes. As I have said in the other passage quoted accurately, I don't wish -- I'm unable to be neutral --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in such situations as camps and massacres and rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is your testimony here today neutral or is it partial on the issue of Omarska and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: My testimony is answering questions. If you're asking me am I going to give you objective facts, yes. If you're asking me am I sitting here neutral between the people who have survived and been bereaved by the camps and the massacres and the people who did it, no, I would be arguing against myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The testimony itself is objective and factual.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I will welcome the opportunity to present you with factual observations that I'd like to ask you about. Now, first of all, if we can digress to another topic dealing with your testimony in the Stakic proceedings. And this was at -- on the 17th of September --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Your Honours, I will not be tendering this document that is on -- on the ELMO, although I am told it is now released in e-court. I think the testimony that I wanted to elicit was able to be elicited, and in keeping with the procedures in this case, since this document is not authored by the witness and he was not aware of all the contents of the same, I don't think I should be tendering it through the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you should first of all take care that the documents you want to use are released on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we sent this into the technical support staff two days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll explore -- if that's the case, then of course we should really --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it's not the Registry's. The ITSS that's at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a closer look into it because that shouldn't take two days I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that once they are uploaded by ITSS, that it is the Defence which finally releases them. That is the information I received from the Registry. It is not the first time that it happens. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. I can also say that the technicians, when they came to see the access that we had on the e-court system, noted that we do not have that ability to release them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish that we did. But I will work on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not going to work on that, you're going to meet with everyone who could tell you and you sort this out so that we don't have to waste time on it in court any further. Again, I leave it open whose mistake it is until now, but it should not happen again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Witness, the question I had for you was relating to an answer you gave in the Stakic transcript on the 17th of December, the 23rd and 24th pages of that day, but I note that the Prosecution exhibit has the entirety of all three days combined so I have to re-adjust to get the page reference for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I missed the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 17th September, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 17th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it is of transcript page 8031. And it's very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the question that was asked of you is: "Is it true, sir, that you do not have any military background or military expertise?" And your answer was: "In service, no. Of warfare, obviously, yes." The question I have for you, sir -- first of all, do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I remember reading it when I went over the testimony. I don't remember the exact moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If you could please clarify for us now, is your answer meant to be understood to signify that you feel you have a military expertise borne of your time as a journalist covering war zones?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: "Expertise" is your word. I have covered in my career --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the wars in Ireland, Iraq many times, and other places. I know war better than I would like to, but I've never served in a military army or service of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you didn't quote a question right, is it. It was "experience" not "expertise." "Is it true, sir, also that you have no political background or experience?" That's the question I have in the exhibit. Nothing about expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I misspoke, Your Honours. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a relevant issue, I understand, in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Your Honours, line 1 of page 8031 does say "military expertise" in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Yes, I see that. I see that later the question is, again, put to the witness. I focussed on 8031 and your question is on 8030. Although the words "military experience" appears on --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 8031 but I looked at that other question. This being clarified, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the reason I asked this is I would like to focus now for a bit on an event that occurred on the convoy that you took from Prijedor to get to Omarska. And first of all could we clarify now, am I correct that the armed escorts that were part of this convoy were from the police of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the convoy in question had a blue police all -- armoured personnel carrier at the head of it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The APC was blue and was under the authority of the police and Mr. Drljaca, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- we're waiting for the transcript, sir, and again I would caution you to please pause after my question before answering as I have a suspicion that we're causing a problem for the translators and for the transcribers. Sir, did this APC also have a heavy machine-gun mounted on it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: As I recall, yes, a round turret.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can have P199. That's the transcript of the Stakic testimony. And the part that I'm referring to is the 16th September, 2002. It is it page 7938 of the transcript and I believe it is page 40 in e-court. Hopefully that will allow us to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, sir, perhaps you can recall this incident. But we're talking about an incident wherein the convoy was fired upon and you were put in a "bad mood about this exchange of fire," and you believed that it wasn't a legitimate exchange of fire with Muslim extremists hiding in the woods. And I believe it's at the bottom of that page, the part that we can't yet see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Or maybe it's the -- is this page 7938 of the transcript? Next page. I apologise. I guess it's page 41. And beginning at line 16, I think, is the -- or line 8, I guess, to have the full --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall this portion of your testimony from the Stakic proceedings?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And have I accurately summarised that you in fact you did not believe that the exchange of fire was a legitimate exchange of fire but rather was a set-up?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I thought it was a prank.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we turn to the next page in the transcript, you give an explanation as to why you thought it was staged and your answer begins: "Yes. It didn't convince. It was all too much overdramatic and all the fire was coming over our heads in exactly the same place. I mean, if you're under fire, the fire is coming at you behind, in front, over, and it's -- I wasn't convinced. It was coming straight over our heads, and it was the way in which these guys with sun-glasses jumped out of the APC. They were returning fire. They were aiming fairly high. It didn't feel right. It didn't feel convincing. I thought to myself then, and I think now, it was an attempt to intimidate us." Do you still hold such a position today, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I've -- I've had no reason to change my mind from the -- the -- as I say, the disposition of the people who were escorting us, were it a real fire-fight, I think it would have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that the armoured personnel carrier machine-gun was firing a sustained stream of fire in the direction of the woods?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't know if I testified to a sustained fire from the APC. I don't think it was that loud or sustained, in my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What about fire from the infantry rifles? Were they sustained bursts rather than individual shots at targets?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: "Sustained" would be too strong a word, I think, for what I recall the amount of shooting going on. It was more bursts, stop, bursts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while the Serb police in sun-glasses, that you say were aiming high, were shooting, were other Serb police trying to advance with their colleagues to forward positions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: This is 20 years ago. We stopped by a bridge. I didn't see any of our escort trying to advance into the woods that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's see if I can refresh your recollection. 1D263 is an excerpt from V000-0910-A which is one of the clips given to us of the ITN footage from that day. And this clip goes from -- I apologise, I have to try and manipulate the computer as I speak. It goes from 18 minutes and 20 seconds to 19 minutes and 7 seconds from the original film, although this 65 ter number is just the portion, these 40 seconds, that I'd like you to review and see if it refreshes your recollection. And I'll caution, there is no sound to this video. And while playing this, sir, could you confirm for us whether this is footage of the fire-fight that you are describing in the transcript section that we just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, having seen this now, does this footage comport with your recollection of the fire-fight seen that we have been discussing from this page in the Stakic transcript?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's the same scene, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you now have a fresher recollected as to whether the personnel that were not firing were trying to advance upon positions towards the woods?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The woods from whence the fire were supposedly coming were to our left, with the camera pointing forward. The man is running back and then across the bridge. He seems to be saying, Carry on, I think. I don't think they're trying to advance towards the -- the -- the alleged firing. There's another man we see who then comes across, anyway, that doesn't seem to be very frightened of any further fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would these --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: -- to take a position of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would these be then flanking positions to the side of the area from which the fire was originating?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The fire is originating from the left as the camera is pointing forward, as I understand it, or sort of left, slightly forward, as I recall. If -- well, the one man on the one hand, he is beckoning to come across the bridge, on the other hand he is running across the bridge, which I wouldn't call an advance particularly. But they're sort of running around it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: -- in a not very organised way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: You've already told us, I belive, in your testimony that you did not have a military background. Have you ever been formally trained in combat tactics?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Prior to your deployment in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, can you recount for us the number of times that you previously found yourself in an active-combat situation or fire-fight?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact number of times, Your Honours. I was working in -- across northern Ireland for many years and I had been in Iraq in 1991, and had worked extensively in Croatia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was about a number. Could you say in the tens, in the hundreds, in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, sir. Tens of different assignments. Hundreds not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Assignments. But to be -- I think the question was about experience in -- in -- in fire-fight, exchange of fire, where you found yourself in such a situation. Is that by the tens, by the hundreds --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's by the tens more than by the hundreds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, before I forget can we tender this video before I ask additional questions, 1D263, into evidence as the next available Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I was informed that the Registry has not been provided with a copy of the video and that there's no surrogate sheet in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Copies were the ones that I had -- that I gave at the beginning of our cross, so that I believe Ms. Stewart has all of them instead of just the one. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what about the Registry who has to keep record of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Registry gets a disc. She has all the discs. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll get that, the usher. And then the surrogate sheet in e-court, do we also get it from Ms. Stewart or?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, the surrogate sheet should be in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And released by whomever?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to see. I do see one surrogate sheet that was released at 259. I don't see if this one is released according to our records as of [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take care that if it's not that it is. By the way, since we're dealing with procedural matters, I stand corrected as far as the reference to the question is, because I saw the similarity on what is found on that page in background, but I missed that the second question was about political background whereas the first question was about military expertise. So I stand corrected that I have not -- I had not sufficiently compared the two questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think we're at the time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. We will take a break after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom. And we'll resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Vulliamy. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, before the break I believe you had recounted for us the many different places where you had been exposed to combat and the number of times exposed to combat. And am I correct that on all those occasions you were - would the terminology be "embedded" as a journalist with armed forces?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I was not embedded with armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Not always. In fact, quite rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In any of those instances, were you embedded with armed forces?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: On a couple of instances in Northern Ireland I would have been accompanied by the British Army. But usually not. In Croatia, on a couple of occasions, with what was then-the Yugoslav national army and the Croatian forces, but not usually. Usually we were just on our own trying to figure things out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: And in Iraq, usually again not, actually. Again, we would be working on our own inasmuch as one could in 1991. But although it sounds a little strange, we were escorted by Saddam Husein's troops south towards Al Basrah in 1991. So it's a mix, but usually not embedded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the course of your experiences that you drew upon to conclude that this incident was staged, did you become familiar or have explained to you the concept of suppressive fire whose objective is to pin down enemy forces with continuous fire rather than to seek to neutralise individual targets from a distance?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'd heard of the term suppressive fire. I'm not entirely sure what it is. The reason I came to the conclusion I did then is I've obviously been shot at quite a lot and the shooting at one tends to not repeatedly go over the top all the time and involve people walking around fairly exposed as in this instance as these men were. The return of fire appeared to be high.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the course of your experiences and in drawing your conclusions, were you familiar with the military tactic known as fire and movement or fire and maneuver that uses suppressive fire or the threat thereof to decrease the enemy's ability to return fire, their unit cohesion, and their morale.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Fire and move, fire and move, fire and move, of course. I think what we discussed in the car was that the fire that was supposedly coming at us was not from people who were genuinely trying to hit our vehicle or the other vehicles and kill us, because if they were they weren't very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the issue at stake, whether this fire was staged or not, that's an impression the witness gained. He explained to us what were the facts on which he based his impression. Nothing more, nothing less. It's perfectly clear that your point is that he may have drawn wrong conclusions and that point is clear to the Chamber. Now since that incident is not central in this case but is, I would say, an aspect, rather, in the margin, the two issues: First, that the witness may have drawn wrong conclusions, and that's the Defence' position, I take it; second, that such wrong conclusions may have been drawn by a person you do not consider to be impartial, are clear. So therefore, if there's -- unless there's anything other, the Chamber suggests that you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would also like to test the witness's recollection of the rate to fire. I have the video-tape with the -- that I found through other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. In the last video I didn't hear any fire at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's because the audio was switched off or whether there was no fire at all. If you say I'd like to further look at the facts on which the witness relied when he gained his impression, then of course please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I'm just checking the latest word. I'm told that the surrogate sheet should be in e-court for this video. It's 1D264 and that should be released, so hopefully we'll have some good news. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, as we wait for this footage which I have to, unfortunately, activate from here, and this is the -- an extract from a video entitled: "Judgement" that we were able to obtain from a third party source. It's from part 1, and it's from 7.26 to 7.57 of that video. And just, sir, for purposes of foundation, do you recall that during the convoy there was another film crew in addition to the ITN crew that was there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, there was another film crew with us throughout from Pale. They were, we were told, from Bosnian Serb television, and some, if not all of them, were wearing military fatigues. And then by the time we got to Trnopolje, there appeared to a fourth camera operating, and I don't know who it was, but that cameraman was also wearing military fatigues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of this tape, Your Honours, there is some English on narration. I'm more interested in the actual ambient sounds of the fire-fight, but I will play it twice, I guess, to comply with the new rules, is that my understanding? I apologise, maybe I should just repeat myself. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the -- the surrogate sheet is for this video that you are going to play now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And for the previous -- or was there a previous where it was still missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There was a previous one. We could check that. That would be -- 1D00263 was the previous one. I'm told they were both [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Because we -- we're still at the stage that the previous one was not released but now both are released; 1D263 and 1D264. We'll now look at the video linked to 1D264.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, my question was I'm more concerned with the ambient sound behind the narration, but since there is narration, do I need to also play this one twice to comply with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends on -- if you say I'm not going rely on the narration at all, it's only the sounds that we're interested in, then I would say that we'll not listen to it. It's perhaps not even necessary to be transcribed because it's not part of the record on which we may rely in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would be my position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed then proceed on this basis. Ms. Bibles seems not to oppose. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then I apologise. We don't seem to have sound coming out of this ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, having reviewed this footage from the other crew that was there, first of all, is this again the same incident that we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Visually, yes. The heavy fire I'm not convinced by. You said you're not concerned with the commentary, but I can't but notice that it talks about loyalist and rebel and Allah. I think this is -- I don't know what emperorsclothes.com is. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I don't accept the audio on that. I recognise the visuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please ignore what was said, as we will do. You say the audio, as far as the sound of firing is concerned, you have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall heavy weaponry of the kind we hear on that track during the -- this episode on our way to Omarska, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I have one additional question in relation to this. The previous video we saw, was there any sound on that, because there was no -- there was no firing to be heard at all. Is it because there is no audio with that material, or is it that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can give you what I know. That video-tape was disclosed to us in that format by the Office of the Prosecutor. There is audio in the section predating that clip. There is audio in the section following that clip, but in that particular clip there is no audio. I don't know whether that is something that's on the original tape or not. That is, unfortunately, the tape that I had when I was preparing for the cross-examinations. And I think it's number V000- -- I don't have the number here. I believe it's V4910-A I think is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bibles, could you inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll have -- we can certainly obtain the original video-tape. I believe this was a compilation video-tape that the first one came from that was used in the Tadic trial. I would have to go back to obtain the original on that to verify whether or not there was audio on that particular clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that could be done overnight, that would be appreciated, so that we know it tomorrow and that we could even verify whether the sound we hear here, if there's any sound on the other one, whether it corresponds, yes or no. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, in this video, visually did we see men trying to manoeuvre to different positions while there was fire being heard, at least on this tape? I take for the moment your objection to the tape, but as far as this tape is concerned, was there visually men moving forward that were not firing while the other -- while there were sounds of other fire taking place?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, we could see, I think, the same man running as on the other film, or one of the two we saw on the other film, and we heard the heavy explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can introduce -- seek to introduce 1D00264 into evidence, and I do understand that I need to provide fresh copies of both of these on individual CDs for the Registrar. I will have that performed this afternoon, so maybe if we MFI it for now until we receive separate discs, that might be the safest course of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, so that we reserve already a number and we have a -- a surrogate sheet in e-court, and we'll wait for the final video to be uploaded -- to be provided to the Registry. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D00264 becomes Exhibit D43, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is marked for identification, waiting for the video to be provided. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vulliamy, I'd like to return to Prijedor for a moment. That is to say, before this convoy left for Omarska. Am I correct that there was another incident where you were glad that your fellow journalist, Tim Juda, was denied the right to join you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. You used the word "glad." That was purely for reasons of professional. He was working for a rival newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say professionally. Did you have a feeling that this report or this trip to Omarska and Trnopolje was going to be a significant boost to your journalistic career?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I did not think in those terms. It's a big question. No. I certainly don't now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the decision to eventually permit your convoy to proceed towards Omarska was relayed to you by Mr. Simo Drljaca as you were waiting outside of the municipal building in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. We had been told to wait outside, and when we were talking with women there, and it was, I think, yes, I recall it was Drljaca who came out and said let's proceed, after whatever negotiations had taken place while we were waiting. The chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The chief of police.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you have mentioned a Colonel Milutinovic. I must confess there's some confusion here I'd like to see if we could clarify it. In your testimony in Stakic, in Kovacevic, in Tadic, in Sikirica, you talk about a Major Milutinovic, whereas in your testimony in the Karadzic proceedings and hear today, you have referred to a Colonel Milutinovic. Could you please provide clarification?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Sorry, Your Honours. I confused the rank. I think he was -- I think he later became a colonel, even a major at the time, and it was Colonel Arsic. I'm confusing the ranks. It's the same man, Milutinovic and Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to Major Milutinovic, at that time that he was part of your convoy, he was affiliated with the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't know which corps he was in at the time, but he was obviously in the army, and he accompanied us to Prijedor from Banja Luka, and thence from Prijedor to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. This morning in direct examination upon questioning by Ms. Bibles, you mentioned that you heard that he went to the General Staff and worked for General Mladic. Am I correct that Major Milutinovic, at this time, was working with the army in Banja Luka, not the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. He was working in the -- with the army in Banja Luka and very briefly we visited whatever facility he was based at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So would you agree with me then that your testimony this morning was again mixing up things that occurred later in time, perhaps in 1996, when this gentleman may have had a rank of colonel and events that happened in 1992 when he was a major with the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I -- I didn't -- I didn't testify that he was -- that he was working at the general headquarters in 1992. We met him in Banja Luka. He was based in Banja Luka. And it was an inquiry about -- well, whatever -- what happened to that man later, that I learnt that he had reportedly - and I can only say reportedly - gone to work at general headquarter. I did not know then whether that was true and I still don't know now. And that he had become a colonel. Hence, my confusion, for which I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing it up for me. Now I believe you mentioned, and I'd like to clarify, that this Major Milutinovic stayed with you up until you came to Trnopolje and that he departed upon your arrival at Trnopolje. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He left us -- he didn't accompany us in the same vehicle from Omarska to Trnopolje that I recall. He accompanied us in the vehicles from Banja Luka to Prijedor, and Prijedor to Omarska. He left, and I don't recall a specific farewell with him, somewhere between Omarska and Trnopolje. Either immediately after Omarska or immediately before Trnopolje. I can't help you with which of those it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can turn -- if we can look at P119 which is the Stakic transcript again. And the section I would like to look is from 16 September 2002, and it is transcript page 7937, which -- I do have the page in e-court. I think it's about the -- I want to say it's about the 30th page in, but I can't be certain of that. It is transcript page 7937 from that transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I was still thinking about you said to the witness that he mixed up what happened at that time or what may have happened later. But when he said -- when the witness said that he went to the General Staff, he was asked whether he had followed the further career of Mr. Milutinovic. So, therefore, I think, in the context, it was perfectly clear that he was not referring to what happened in 1992 but what may have happened in the further career apart from that the witness said that he has no - that's what he heard but he doesn't know whether it's accurate or not, and then to say you are mixing up what happened earlier and later might not be totally fair to the witness if the question was about the further career, which is unlimited in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I was not able to review the transcript during the break as I was dealing with the issue of whether exhibits were released -- documents were released or not in e-court, so I was working off of memory of the answer rather than the question, and indeed the confusion as to between colonel and major was impetus for that discussion. I'm glad we've been able to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As soon as you start blaming a witness for mixing up matters, then you should find time. I mean, it took me two seconds to find the source, and then you should accurately check whether you -- for good reasons blame the witness for mixing up matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on this page a little bit tighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at lines 10 and 11 here, and this time I don't think I'm misspeaking, is this your testimony in the Stakic proceedings wherein you claim it was Major Milutinovic that told Tim Juda and the other news journalists that they could not accompany you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I read the testimony. We -- we were waiting to go. The two men came out together. Juda arrived. And I don't recall -- I remember it was Drljaca who said, Let's go to Omarska. I don't recall now from the actual event whether it was Milutinovic who told Juda that he couldn't go. But I'll stand by the testimony which is ten years ago that it was. There was a discussion as to who or who was not part of Dr. Karadzic's party. That was the issue at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's see if I can refresh your recollection with your testimony from another proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could look at the Karadzic transcript, which is in e-court as 1D00242. It is from the 9th of November 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a extract from it or is it the whole video?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe it's the whole for now for showing the witness, because we weren't sure which sections we would show, but I will not tender the whole transcript obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- put it clearly on the record, one might wonder whether it's any need at all to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- have it admitted into evidence. Please find the right place you want to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The 11th page in e-court. And, again, this is the 9th of November, 2011, transcript page 21043. But it is the 11th page in e-court, and it starts at line 12, and I will read it into the record, Your Honours, so that we do not have to clutter the record with transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, it begins like this: "Q. But were told they couldn't? "A. Yes, the matter was adjudicated by Simo Drljaca that they couldn't find -- the reason given was they weren't part of Dr. Karadzic's party. They weren't going at his invitation and on his authority." And for the record, the prior discussion was talking about a journalist from "The Times" and a colleague from "Liberation." Are these the individuals Tim Juda and the other journalist who we've been discussing, from "The Times" and from the "Liberation" news organisations.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, Tim Juda from "The Times" and the man who's name I don't know from "Liberation."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does this refresh your recollection of who actually gave the decision that these men could not join the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. And I'll stand by both of them because this is a conversation. These two men are organising our visit, they're working together. There's a collection around the vehicles, they're talking, they're chatting, and it was from them, from Drljaca, from Milutinovic, I don't know if Kovacevic was there. I don't think he was. No, you can't go. You're not in Karadzic's party.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I indicated, I will not be tendering this transcript into the record unless the Prosecution thinks it needs to for contextual purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles is nodding no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the section from the Stakic case that we just had on the screen before this one, that was page 7937, therein you testified that you met Milutinovic there, then. But I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me move on. Let me move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. If we could move back now to the time-period before this decision was made and before the convoy set forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were in a meeting within the municipal building in Prijedor that -- in which Mr. Drljaca, Mr. Stakic, Mr. Kovacic, and others talked with you about your request to visit Omarska and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for reference this is at transcript 7832 of the 16th September, 2002, Stakic transcript, so it should be five pages beyond the last Stakic entry that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask you: During that meeting, am I correct that you were shown a video-tape and comments were made by the participants about a video that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we talking about 7832 or 7932?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 7832, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for me the redacted transcript starts at 7898 or we are in the Stakic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Stakic, that's correct. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My transcript starts at least as -- the redacted transcript starts at -- with the blackened out 7898, so I wonder whether you are referring to -- when you said five pages beyond the last Stakic entry we had, and that was in the 7-9 series.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It must be then 7932. You're accurate. I must have a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll follow it from 7932.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Down further. It might be the previous page. But this is -- this is leading -- this is leading to the next question. I was just phrasing the -- the meeting for the witness, so if -- we could refer to it if we need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall during that meeting there was a video-tape that was shown to you that consisted of footage of caches of weapons that were said to have been captured from armed Muslim insurgents in the villages surrounding the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. It was a fairly -- yes, I recall it well. It was a very rasping video in which it showed that they had found weapons and they'd found copies of the Qur'an in people's houses. Those were the points that were being emphasised by the people at the -- on the committee we were with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think we want the -- just the end of the prior page leading on to this page. If we could have both pages up in e-court, then we can follow along with the brief selection that I want to ask about what the officials said would be found. There we go. I'm starting from page -- I guess it's 7831, then, line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 7-9, again, yes, I apologise. 7931, line 13 onward, and it'll bleed over onto the next page. The next page 7932, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first -- let me just try and read this to highlight the portions that I'd like to have your comment on. This is president Stakic now speaking: "I am glad you have come here to this situation here, but I am sorry because the international publicity was not -- or publications, pub, was not int. two to three months ago in this area. At that time, there was heavier fighting than now. Two years ago, elections. There was -- government was half/half Serbians and Muslims. I was negotiating two sides, Serbs and the Muslims. Get try to agree, the other side to live in peace together. What we are looking for today. We think we have problems from the Muslim extremists here, not with the Muslim population. We asked the Muslims not to leave this area, but to live together with us. Serbs are not doing any genocide to other people. "We cannot make a nation. It is very difficult for such a country to exist. The other side buying weapons all the time. Croatian and Muslim extremists. We have a doc, a Kozarski. There are -- there were 3.500 armed people. We have the names and the weapons they have got. We have two tapes and by the Muslims how they were prepared for this war. Even we try very hard to not. They started to kill the Serbian people in this area. They made barricades. Beginning of May, on the main and side roads. Green headbands and berets. SDA with a line through, Serbian people saw what was going to be and know what was in the Second World War. Started to protect themselves, their house, in this area. We defend us from the first. A clash from the other side. In that documentation, from all that we saw, from papers and documents, we had a fear what could be done to us." Now this particular section that I've highlighted from your testimony, that has been accepted in this case now as well, am I correct that this was your recitation of your shorthand notes from the meeting that you had in the municipal assembly in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, correct. This is my reading for the Chamber the exact transcript of my shorthand notes of how Mr. Stakic interpreted the situation or, rather, what he wanted us to hear from him. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And prior to arriving in Prijedor in August of 1992, did you by way of research or other means, have occasion to find out about the attack on the town centre that took place in May of 1992 when an armed group of approximately 200 Croats and Muslims attacked down-town Prijedor and attempted to take over the town, killing several Serbs in the process?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Prior to, no. Since, if I can continue, yes, I have heard about that incident. But it pales in -- pales in comparison to what I have also found to have happened in the other direction. And I have also heard about a barricade, as well. He says they made barricades. I've heard about one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would that be the one on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Hambarine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion several JNA soldiers were killed by these armed Bosnian Muslim individuals including ethnic Serbs and ethnic non-Serbs, as I believe two of the JNA soldiers were Croats?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't know the details of the -- or the numbers of casualties on either side in Hambarine. But everything that we saw that day, and everything that I have worked on over the 20 years since - and there's been a lot of it - militates very -- very much in the opposite direction as to how the violence was apportioned between these two sides. That's to understate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again is that you being neutral or impartial?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sir, this testimony is completely impartial. If the words you cited earlier from the time of war where - the language, perhaps a little strong - it was all happening. You're using these words. It's all much more heavy-hearted now and sadder, but I'm -- I'm giving evidence, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: -- summarising my work. I'm trying to answer your question. I, for what it's worth, know now, impartially, on the basis of facts and testimonies I've heard - and I've taken this extremely seriously and heavy-heartedly - over the years that Mr. Stakic's account of the direction in which the violence was going in that area was untrue. That the version of things he was giving us that day was not true. Although the incidents he describes in Prijedor -- sorry, that you asked about in Prijedor and a barricade I know now was true. Sorry about the rambling answer, but you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's okay. I let you finish so you'd get your full say.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sir, you're asking me, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I direct you with another question?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Stakic's assertion that the Croats and Muslims were buying lots of weapons and that there were 3.500 armed men in Kozarac. Do you have any knowledge about that allegation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: At the time, no. Since, yes. I do not think there were 3.000 armed men in Kozarac. I do understand there was some resistance from the police station at first, but it was very quickly and thoroughly overwhelmed by artillery bombardments and the clearing -- cleansing of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you a witness to any of that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, sir, but I was a witness on that day, August the 5th, to the result of it. The place had been almost gutted by explosions and fire and there was nobody there apart from a few Serbs who were remaining, as was explained by Mr. Milutinovic, in fact, and I did have occasion to go back into 1996 to see that Kozarac was almost entirely deserted and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you, since you mentioned Mr. Milutinovic: On the convoy to Omarska, am I correct that you also passed villages that had white towels or flags hanging from structures, houses, minarets, et cetera, and that those villages were entirely intact and it was explained to that you those villages had decided to peacefully co-exist with the Serb authorities in Prijedor and there was no armed action in those areas. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We were -- it was -- yes, it does. Thank you. It was explained to us that those who had agreed to hang white sheets or pillow cases from their windows or whatever had accepted the new order, and it was also explained that they had agreed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are the --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The villages were not entirely intact, by the way. You said entirely. They weren't. Some houses in all these communities we went through had been bombed out or shelled or burned, but not all of them and not those from which the sheets were hanging.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And likewise, were there not Croatian villages that likewise were -- remained loyal to the Prijedor authorities, the Serb authorities, and did not have combat take place in those villages?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't know then specifically about the Croatian villages in the area, nor which they were. I now know which ones you're referring to, and they are not as -- they're not totally destroyed like Kozarac and the villages around Kozarac, but I do not at all -- the Croats that I've spoken to do not give any indication that they were loyalable -- loyal to the Prijedor authorities. They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask you this question: Were there not Croatians were that mobilised or called up and were part of the army of the Republika Srpska in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: If you say so, yes. There was a lot of -- there was cross -- people fought -- a lot of people fought for armies which were not necessarily of their religious side. Tens of thousands of Serbs fought for the "government side" or, as they called it, the republican side. I don't know specifically about Croats fighting for the Republika Srpska. If you say so, it may be. But I was back in one of the Croatian villages that you're talking about, called Ljubija, just this summer, and they were -- all the Croats from that village were -- were removed from the village. Forcibly. Via the camps, many of them. Or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, sir, did you eye-witness any of this that you just mentioned in the last two minutes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. I hope I made it clear. This was going back to -- to -- to gather deeper and further information on the places you're asking me about. I hope I made it clear that at the time I was not aware of these Croatian villages or indeed which ones they were. The village -- the towns that we passed on the way to Prijedor from Banja Luka were Kozarac and the surrounding communities, which were very, very, heavily, almost entirely destroyed. And then subsequently on the way from Prijedor to Omarska, we saw other villages which were partially destroyed and those that -- houses that weren't destroyed had the sheets and the pillow cases hanging from them. I hope I've made that clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have. I've --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: -- that the reference to the Croatian villages was upon my return just actually this year to research them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you gave testimony just now about how those villages became empty, and I'm asking you, sir, is that something that you are a witness to or is that the result of you talking to people? I'm trying to figure if you are an expert witness or a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, no. I was a witness to some people going back this year to the houses that they used to live in that were taken from them, from which they were expelled via Omarska in which Serbs were now living. But I wasn't there in 1992 when it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must insist that pauses are made between question and answer and answer and question, because otherwise we'll lose too much of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise and I will try on my side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, me too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can move up just to finish up on Dr. Stakic's words here. Is there two other -- there's a few other lines that deal directly with Omarska and Trnopolje that I'd like to ask you about, and this on the same section continuing from line 10 through line 18 of the transcript. "There's no conc. camps exists. Only transit camps" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue. I see there is "no conc. camps," which I understand to refer to Mr. Stakic saying that there were concentration camps and that's not what you read, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm reading the transcript. I have to read what's in the transcript, and the transcript says "conc." because this is the shorthand of the witness, and I cannot -- I obviously think it means "concentration" as well but I cannot testify about that. I have to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Then I missed it. I thought initially that I read on the transcript or I heard there are no camps, but I may have misheard. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. "I'll start from the beginning again, sir. "There is no conc.," and it's spelled C-O-N-C, "camps exists. Only transit camps that we put some of the refugees in their camps to protect them. And some come by themselves. The refugees who want to leave this area. Some of them want to go back to Bosnia, Izetbegovic country. And it is provided for most of them to go there, but there is many of the Muslim people, they don't want to go and live in that country. They want to go to Croatia, Austria, Germany. Now we are negotiate with UNPROFOR, and int. cross to provide those people with all the docs. queueing to get the documents to go abroad."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we could first clarify the first line of this quotation from your shorthand notes. By "conc. camps" are we talking about concentration camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could clarify also by the abbreviation "int. cross," are we talking about the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, during your time at Trnopolje did you have occasion to verify these words of Dr. Stakic and hear that there were, in fact, persons, refugees who came to Trnopolje themselves?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Some of them, a few of them, yes. And it was fairly obvious why. We had just driven by their houses that had been blown up or shelled or burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you -- do you consider that this part of Mr. Stakic's address was plausible and truthful in so far as you previously said that the other part you did not believe was not true?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think that by the time we got to Omarska, it was becoming clear that this was not a transit camp. It was much worse than that. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question was with regard to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, with -- to Trnopolje. Well, no, he is talking about no concentration camps exist, only transit --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: -- camps --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: -- and my answer to you is that Omarska was clearly not a transit camp. So no, he did not convince me on that score, nor does that version of things convince me since.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, well let's --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: To answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's see about seem of these parts where you consider that Mr. Stakic's account was untruthful. If we could explore your prior testimony in another case as it relates to weapons that the Bosnian Muslims and Croats were buying, which you have now testified was not -- part of the not truthful part of Mr. Stakic's statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could call up 1D242. This is the Karadzic transcript again. And this time it is page 39 in e-court, and it should be transcript 21072 from the original transcript from November of 2011, November 9th, 2011, and, again, it should be the 39th page in e-court. The next page, I apologise. 21072. And if we could start at line 15 and onward.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, here, Mr. Karadzic is questioning you about things in your first book: "Seasons in Hell." And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- yes, it has been resolved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for -- again, I do not intend to tender the entire transcript, so I will just read in the question and answer that I am going to be asking this witness about. It starts at line 12 here, and the question from Mr. Karadzic is: "Q. Let's finish with the book, according to the Trial Chamber's guidance. Let's look at page 11 in e-court, please. Can the left-hand side be displayed. "You're talking about the embargo, about the difficulties experienced by the Muslim side with regard to the purchasing of weapons, and then at the bottom of the page you say that you were aware of a perverse smuggling route along which guns, paid for by the Muslims, using money from Turkey and the Arab countries, would arrive at the Croatian port of Rijeka. And then can we look at the top of the right-hand side page. And then you describe how the Croats would take a half cut; is that correct? "A. As I understood it, from a number of sources, Bosnian government, military, HVO Croatian military, and international intelligence, this was the deal that pertained to some of the arms shipments. I can't speak for all of them. That as the front and central Bosnian, at least, became progressively cut off, they would get a quarter of the weapons that would arrive in Rijeka, or indeed later by plane, and that there would be a ... commission, if you like, of 50 per cent to the HV and another 25 percent for the HVO." Now, sir, is this testimony from the Karadzic proceedings something that you still stand by?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is much later in the war, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the HV would be the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: HV is the Army of Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And HVO would be the armed part of --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would be the armed part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna that existed on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mention among your sources, quote/unquote, international intelligence. Can you please identify for us the international intelligence service that you had as a source for this information? And if you feel we must go in private session to do so, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary to go into private session at all. They were Danish and some British. But I didn't set much store by the British, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to be clear, how frequent were your contacts with these sources in the -- in these intelligence agencies, the Danish and the British agencies?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Infrequent. Very infrequent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you read a part of the Karadzic transcript into the record. Also my first question was: What's the time-frame, what are we talking about? And then apparently at that moment everyone is looking at page 11 in e-court, because that's where the story starts. But I've got no idea what is on that page 11 in e-court, what the document is they apparently are reading from. Whether that's the book, although it's indicated that they want to finish with the book. I've got no idea. If you could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can try and clarify it with the witness, Your Honours. I have no personal knowledge since we do not have access to the materials that were used in the Karadzic trial as of yet to be able to verify all this. I tried to find the book by Mr. Vulliamy. I did not have a copy in the sufficient time they put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this mean that you put this question to the witness without even having the slightest idea of what was on screen at that moment in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I -- from the transcript it's clear that they're talking about the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But I don't have a physical copy of the book so that I have to ask the witness about that. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The book is what book?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Seasons in Hell," written by Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So page 11, you say you have no access to it, but I take it that page 11 of this book is publicly available.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not on the Internet or here, but, yes, there are books that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, sometimes you still have to buy them in a bookstore, or in libraries sometimes they have books. But apparently you have not checked that. Then I can immediately ask Mr. Vulliamy: This part of the Karadzic transcript, was the questions that -- or what was on the screen, was that your book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if I'm told that this is a quote from the book, I wrote it nearly 20 years ago, it is available, then, fine. But the account of how this arms smuggling worked in about 1994, beginning of 1995, is accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Bibles, you were on your feet as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour. "Seasons in Hell" written by this witness is available in the ICTY library.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the ICTY library has the book, which may assist you. Then I think we should take a break at this point in time. We would have half an hour left after the break. Mr. Vulliamy, would you be the first to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break, and we will resume at 13 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, in terms of scheduling next week, Your Honour, because of a personal matter related to one of our staff, I'm seeking to reverse the order of the first and second witnesses so that the first witness on Monday would be RM051 and the second witness would be Mr. Selak. I've spoken with my colleagues on the Defence and they have informed me that they have no objection, so with the Court's permission we'd like to make that switch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a look at it. But as -- usually there are no objections against such technical changes if the parties agree on it. But we'll have a further look at it and let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please be seated, Mr. Vulliamy. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think as I indicated I would not be seeking to tender this transcript selection into evidence, and I believe that Mr. Vulliamy has now added that this was sometime later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct to understand to that arms transfer was later in the war period?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It pertaining during a period of the war when there was a lot of combat, ironically, given its content between the Bosnian government side and the Croats, the HVO, that we were talking about. And the Bosnians in central -- in the central part of the country were cut off, and this was when -- when they could get reference this is how it worked. They would have to sort of agree to their enemy taking a cut of the shipment, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the witness referred to 1994, beginning of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to another part of -- that I believe relates to what Mr. Stakic was talking about in the -- in the discussion that you had the shorthand for. And this relates to Trnopolje, and, at this time I would like to play more of the footage from the other TV crew that was at Trnopolje. That is, the Serb TV unit that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at this time, I would call up 65 ter number 1D259, and this is selections from, again, that same video judgement, and there are three separate sections. I propose we deal with each section individually. And in the manner that Your Honours had suggested, I will first play that segment one time over to allow the translation verification to occur, and then I will play the second time and ask the questions that I have with the witness, and we'll do each section separately and then I will, depending on the answers I get, probably tender this -- these three excerpts together as one number, which I believe those are on a disc that is in the possession of Madam Registrar so that hopefully will work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic, could at any point in time the Chamber be informed about who produced it. There was word about crews being in uniforms. The Chamber would be interested in knowing about the background, as we know everything about Mr. Vulliamy's background now, about the background of those who produced this material --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With that mind, I have in the first clip I have the actual beginning of the tape which gives the copyright information, and I have planned to endeavour to try to bring the persons that made the video as witnesses in this trial or -- or to present evidence of that nature. Obviously Mr. Vulliamy has given what he can. I cannot offer more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sooner or later we'll receive more information. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Reporter: Two film crews visiting a humanitarian refugee centre in the village of Trnopolje, some 3 to 4 kilometres away from Omarska. The centre was mainly used by people in transit. They were trying to get away from the fighting and needed a place to stay during their travels. Our reporter, Mr. Bodjanac [phoen], talked to some of these people who had escaped the war zone." "Reporter: [No interpretation]."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll play it again. Have the booth been provided with transcripts in two languages?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you shouldn't present videos without transcripts if you want to rely on the text spoken. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's not been the practice in other cases that I've been involved in, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because we only have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- something we should discuss then. It has been practice in -- as far as I remember all of the cases I was involved in. But if there is a different practice, then we should clarify this as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. Because the one problem we have, Your Honours, is we -- certain of the videos we have from the Prosecution we have translation -- transcripts someone has prepared, but with respect to material that we bring in from other sources, unless we prepare transcripts, I don't know. Would that be acceptable to just prepare -- to have counsel or staff prepare transcripts or translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As long as it is done with the required accuracy. And then, of course, you should present it for translation or have it translated in whatever way. Could we exceptionally, apparently there being a miscommunication, could we proceed and see whether -- whether it works at this moment. It will be discussed soon so as to resolve it on a long-term basis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May it be noted that the quality of the sound on the video-clip is not good enough for us to actually understand what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean in the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest that -- was there ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There were subtitles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's subtitled so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The first two sections are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order not to get stuck, the Chamber would like to proceed on the basis of the subtitles which is, of course, a bit odd because then it would be translated into B/C/S again, but the Defence team has every opportunity after that to see whether the badly understandable B/C/S version then is produced in such a way that we can work on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it perhaps assist, I can leave this part for tomorrow since we will be going into tomorrow as well and I can move on to another section. Overnight I'm sure I can prepare a transcript of the sections and then that might make it easier for ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If you say you can deal with it tomorrow, then you are encouraged to -- to proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honours, then, for the sake of efficiency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Mladic again speak at such a volume that it does not come through my earphones where I'm listening to the English. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could leave this aside, sir, and move back to our discussion of Trnopolje. Am I correct that there were not many persons that you would consider guards at this location? Again, we're talking about Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: There were quite a number of guards but not as many as there were at Omarska so far as I could gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: There were guards around the compound we saw in one of the earlier photos. Quite a few of them, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that quite a few of those guards came with the convoy that you -- quite a few of the people from the video that you saw earlier came in the convoy that you came with? They were escorts of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: A few of them, but there were guards who were based at Trnopolje also. Obviously. It was a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that there were sections of Trnopolje that were not fenced in?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: There were some sections around the buildings that were not fenced in and then there was the compound that we pulled up besides that was fenced in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
